justifications.functional_suitability: Catalogue Management Component handles item CRUD in PostgreSQL, and Catalogue & Search Service fetches digital assets via Digital Repository / DRM Provider, so R-01 (physical and digital items) is covered. Circulation & User Service adds loans and fines. Gaps: no explicit physical vs digital item model.
justifications.performance_efficiency: Search Query Component uses Elasticsearch, Search Indexer Component syncs asynchronously via Kafka, CloudFront caches assets, React Query caches client-side, PgBouncer pools connections, and RUM monitoring exists. Gaps: no explicit autoscaling, and no load-test or latency budget for the 800 ms P99 target.
justifications.compatibility: Integrates with External Payment Gateway (REST/TLS), Digital Repository / DRM Provider (async REST), External Notification Service (mTLS), and standard protocols (OIDC, gRPC, Avro, OTLP). Gaps: no anti-corruption adapter for DRM and no standard library interoperability protocols such as MARC or Z39.50.
justifications.usability: Web Application provides separate patron and staff views via Router & Layout Component and a Circulation & Self-Service Portal Module, plus Core Web Vitals monitoring. Gaps: no accessibility, mobile or multilingual mechanisms, and no dedicated staff or kiosk interface.
justifications.reliability: Kafka Broker Nodes span 3 AZs, Multi-AZ Redis serves rate limiting, Retry & DLQ Manager Component and the Search Indexer DLQ handle failures, and asynchronous decoupling is used. Gaps: no explicit database replication or backup/failover, no circuit breakers, and no DR/RTO targets.
justifications.security: Authentication & Authorization Filter does JWT validation, with OIDC and HttpOnly cookies in Authentication & Session Manager, mTLS gRPC, TLS 1.3, WAF/DDoS at CloudFront, Secrets Manager, Kafka SASL/ACLs, tokenized payments, PII-scrubbed DLQ, audit logs via Kafka, and Zod validation.
justifications.maintainability: Clear service decomposition (Catalogue & Search, Circulation & User, Notification Worker), event-driven decoupling via Apache Kafka, Schema Registry, Flyway/Liquibase migrations, and OTel tracing. Gaps: shared Database across services creates coupling, and mixed Go/Java stacks plus inconsistent technology labels.
justifications.portability: Terraform/OpenTofu and open technologies (PostgreSQL, Kafka, Kong, Elasticsearch) help portability. However, heavy AWS reliance (MSK, RDS, CloudFront, Secrets Manager, Glue) creates lock-in, and there are no containerisation or orchestration details.

sensitivity_points: Elasticsearch deployment ambiguous (modelled as Database relation)
tradeoffs: Eventual-consistency indexing vs low-latency dedicated search
Gateway JWT and mTLS hops add latency
PERF-01.justification: Dedicated Elasticsearch search path, stateless JWT validation, and rate limiting support low latency. But no search-result caching, replica/shard sizing, autoscaling or load test evidence for 2,000 concurrent users; P99 is unproven.

sensitivity_points: Indexer consumer lag under write bursts
Indexing load competing with search queries on Elasticsearch
tradeoffs: Async indexing decouples writes but delays searchability
DLQ protects the pipeline but can leave items unindexed
PERF-02.justification: Writes go to PostgreSQL and are asynchronously indexed through Kafka, with a DLQ, keeping the read path separate. A 5-minute freshness is plausible. Lag monitoring, DLQ replay and index/search isolation are not specified.

sensitivity_points: Elasticsearch cluster topology and replicas undefined
tradeoffs: Replica count raises resilience but increases cost and indexing load
Kafka decoupling aids loans but not search
AVAIL-01.justification: Elasticsearch has no stated clustering, replicas or failover, so a node failure could interrupt search. Circulation uses PostgreSQL and Kafka (3 AZ), but database HA/Multi-AZ is not stated and no explicit loan durability mechanism is given. Weakly addressed.

sensitivity_points: Number of service instances not specified
No load balancer or health checks modelled
tradeoffs: Static SPA via CDN is highly available
Stateless services scale but require session handling via cookies
AVAIL-02.justification: The SPA is served by a CDN, so the front end is resilient, and the gateway rate limiter is Multi-AZ. But the brief's 'portal instance' failure is not addressed: no replicas, load balancing, health checks or orchestration is modelled. Loan durability depends on an unspecified database HA.

sensitivity_points: Provider integration is embedded in Catalogue & Search Service
tradeoffs: Fewer containers is simpler but couples integrations to the catalogue
Single DRM interface hides provider differences, if one exists
MOD-01.justification: A single DRM/repository link exists, but no dedicated integration component or provider-adapter abstraction. A new provider would likely change the catalogue service internals, not one confined component. Feasible with moderate rework.

sensitivity_points: Loan rules location undefined; likely hardcoded in Go
No rules engine or configuration store
tradeoffs: Hardcoded rules are fast and simple but need redeploys
Configurable rules add flexibility but complexity
MOD-02.justification: No rules engine, configuration service, or per-library policy store is modelled. Loan rules are implicitly within Loan Management code, so differing rules would need code changes and redeployment, contrary to the runtime configuration requirement.

sensitivity_points: External providers' hosting regions are unspecified
CloudFront is global with edge locations outside the EU
Egress controls described only for notifications
tradeoffs: Managed AWS services ease operations but depend on region configuration
Third-party notification delivery may leave the EU
SEC-01.justification: RDS Frankfurt, MSK and Frankfurt endpoints support EU storage, and egress filtering exists. But no preventive guardrails (SCPs, region policies) are shown, CloudFront edge caching is global, and external notification/payment providers are not constrained to the EU.

sensitivity_points: Object-level ownership check not modelled in Loan Management
tradeoffs: Gateway-only JWT validation is fast but cannot enforce per-record ownership
Audit via Kafka is decoupled but asynchronous
SEC-02.justification: JWT validation and claims propagation authenticate patrons, and gateway access logs go to Kafka. But no component enforces patron-to-loan ownership authorization or explicitly logs denied attempts, leaving the core requirement unaddressed.

elements: Performance Monitoring and Real User Monitoring
